doc.title: Phil Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 27, 2023

title: Writing 'Mercy Mercy Mercy' for Buddy Rich
summary: Rowe asks about the key change; Wilson says he wrote three charts in a week for Buddy Rich, including his first rock chart.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I wanted to show you, I came across a program of a local high school band, this is in Central New York, the Whitesboro Jazz Ensemble concert, July 15, 1969. And the first piece on it — “Mercy Mercy Mercy” Joe Zawinul arranged by P. Wilson.

Ta-da. You know that was like a hot chart and still is of course. And I remember playing it and I was and still am a huge Cannonball Adderley fan so when it got to that part in your arrangement where it abruptly changed keys I was like whoa — what was that?

That was my first rock chart. And I’m sitting there — Buddy really wanted to do that. It was his doing. Cannonball had that album, the single rather, and it was kind of like a church scene if you remember. It was rumored — and I’m — he said that’s the only — I wrote three in one week which is for me unheard of. But this was Buddy Rich and he was playing at Lennie’s on the Turnpike, he’s going to be there for one week, I better take advantage of the moment and come up with something. So I wrote “Chelsea Bridge” for him and I wrote “Mr. Lucky” [scats] from an old TV show. And I wrote “Mercy Mercy.”

And the “Chelsea Bridge,” that’s right, “Lush Life,” and “Mercy.” And the last one — actually I wasn’t used to the straight eighth notes at the time [scats] and writing all those damn things out, which takes some time. And so [scats] You know? And then there’s that celebratory kind of sound, you know [scats].
But why did you change keys? Just because you could?

This is going to be like four minutes in the key of B flat. It gives a little buzz but just move it up to D flat there for a minute. And then we kind of built it [scats] up a half step [scats] which is like that’s from “My Fair Lady” that’s from [scats] and home again, yeah.
